claims.text: The starting powders are elemental Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti mixed in equiatomic proportions.
Slow thermal equilibration of the equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi powder mixture promotes brittle intermetallic or HCP phases.
Twenty hours of high-energy ball milling induces severe plastic deformation and amorphization.
The proposed SPS cycle is 950°C, a 100°C/min heating rate, a 5-minute hold, and 50 MPa uniaxial pressure.
A controlled displacement rate corresponding to an approximately 10^-3 s^-1 strain rate is suitable during densification.
A vacuum below 10^-3 Pa prevents oxidation during SPS.
Milling-generated dislocations and grain boundaries lower the activation energy for nucleation of an FCC solid solution.
Milling-generated defects raise the kinetic barrier to diffusion-controlled formation of Ti-rich HCP phases.
The rapid SPS thermal cycle limits grain growth and solute segregation.
Mechanical alloying creates a supersaturated solid solution with a high defect density.
Formation of a Ti-rich HCP phase requires long-range Ti diffusion.
Rapid heating and a short dwell kinetically favor a metastable nanocrystalline FCC/BCC solid solution over Ti-rich HCP phase separation.
Applied pressure closes pores before significant grain coarsening occurs.
The proposed process produces a relative density above 99.5%.
The proposed process produces an average grain size of 20-50 nm.
The resulting microstructure is an FCC-dominant matrix containing 5-10% BCC phase and no consequential brittle HCP phase.
The processed alloy has a Vickers hardness of 450-550 HV.
Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi has 2-5% porosity, a coarse single-phase FCC structure, and a hardness of 150-200 HV.
Sintering above 1050°C promotes HCP formation and grain growth, causing the strategy to fail.
The hardness increase in the metastable FCC/BCC material is attributable primarily to grain refinement rather than solute strengthening.

contradictions.description: The design specifies nanoindentation at 10 mN with a 10-second dwell, whereas the measurement list specifies Vickers hardness. These are distinct indentation methods, and no Vickers load or dwell is provided.
